headline: Kurōto is 玄 (kuro, “deep, profound”) plus 人 (-uto, “person”), an old root form of 人 (hito).
Shiyōnin is 使用 (shiyō) plus 人 (-nin).
Onbu is from おぶう (obuu).
Hyotto has an onomatopoeic ひょ (hyo) element, plus と (to), an adverb-forming particle.
レギュラー is from English regular.
チェンジ is borrowed from English change.
Nukedasu is 抜け (nuke, the stem of 抜ける (nukeru, “to be extracted, to come out”)) plus 出す (dasu, “to take out”).
Taimen is from the Middle Chinese compound 對面 (MC twojH mjienH).
Nebiki is 値 (ne, “price”) plus 引き (hiki, “reducing”), with hiki voiced to biki by rendaku.
Tonda is the past or perfective of 飛ぶ (tobu, “to deviate from common sense”), and is unrelated to とんでもない (tondemonai, “outrageous”).
Kiwamete is from 極める (kiwameru).
Soshi is ultimately from Middle Chinese 阻止 and is first attested in 1827.
Makanau is from Old Japanese, attested in the Kojiki (712) with the spelling 麻迦那波而.
アマチュア is from English amateur.
Kenzen was first used by Sugita Gendan to translate Dutch gezond, in the 1867 book 健全学.
In hanran, 反 is a daiyōji replacing 叛.
Nagashi is the continuative stem of the verb 流す (nagasu).
ユニフォーム is borrowed from English uniform.
Ogoru, “to give (someone) a treat”, is a doublet of 驕る (ogoru, “to be arrogant”).
セクション is from English section.
カクテル is borrowed from English cocktail.
In kikaku, 画 is a daiyōji replacing 劃.
Chanoma is 茶 (cha, “tea”) plus 間 (ma, “space”).
Kakei is 家 plus 計.
Nippon is a phonetic variant of Nihon that keeps the p sound.
Tsukaeru is from Old Japanese, appears in the Man'yōshū of 759, and is cognate with 使う (tsukau, “to use”).
Hadashi was originally 肌 (hada, “skin”) plus 足 (ashi, “foot”).
センス is from English sense.
In hanshoku, 繁 is a daiyōji replacing 蕃.
Jūgyōin is 従業 (jūgyō, “employment”) plus 員 (-in, “member”).
